pos: n. (Robert Hall, 1764–1831, English Baptist preacher of Cambridge, Leicester, and Bristol, and advocate of open communion)
etymology: Germanic Hrodebert, bright fame; English Hall, a dweller at the hall.
biblical_def: Robert Hall was the son of Robert Hall of Arnesby, whose Help to Zion's Travellers (1781) had helped free English Particular Baptists from the high Calvinism that would not invite sinners to Christ. The younger Hall was trained at Bristol Baptist Academy and King's College, Aberdeen, and became the most celebrated pulpit orator of his generation in any English denomination. He was pastor at St Andrew's Street, Cambridge, from 1791 to 1806, where university men came to hear him; at Harvey Lane, Leicester, from 1807 to 1826, in William Carey's former pulpit; and at Broadmead, Bristol, from 1826 until his death. His sermon Modern Infidelity Considered (1800) was a powerful reply to the atheism of the French Revolution. He suffered two breakdowns of mental health in 1804 and 1805, and lifelong physical pain. In 1815 he published On Terms of Communion, arguing that churches should admit to the Lord's Table all who give evidence of faith in Christ, whether or not they had been baptized as believers; Joseph Kinghorn of Norwich answered him for the strict communion position, and the controversy divided English Baptists for a century. His preaching aimed at what Paul called “demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1Co 2:4), and his plea was Paul's: “receive ye one another, as Christ also received us” (Rom 15:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines communion as fellowship, and in the church as the celebration of the Lord's Supper.
webster_full: COMMU'NION, n. Fellowship; intercourse between two persons or more; union in religious worship, or in doctrine and discipline. The act of communicating the sacrament of the eucharist.
OR'ATOR, n. A public speaker; one who pronounces a discourse publicly on some subject.
INFIDEL'ITY, n. Disbelief of the inspiration of the Scriptures, or the divine origin of christianity; unbelief.
scriptures: Rom 15:7
Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God.
And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:
Act 2:41
Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
corruption_summary: The great Baptist orator who opened the Lord's Table to unbaptized believers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Hall's case for open communion was an argument from Christian love and from Rom 14:1, “Him that is weak in the faith receive ye” (Rom 14:1), and it was made by a man of deep piety. The strict Baptists who answered him argued from the apostolic order, in which those who “gladly received his word were baptized” (Act 2:41) and then continued in the breaking of bread; baptism precedes the Supper in the New Testament without exception.

The principle to recover is that charity and order are both apostolic, and that the question between Hall and Kinghorn was how to keep both, not whether to choose one. A church that tells a believer it cannot have him at the table must still call him brother; a church that admits all believers must still teach that Christ commanded believers to be baptized.
roots_summary: Greek proslambano (G4355), to receive; apodeixis (G585), demonstration; dokimazo (G1381), to examine.
roots_lines: Greek proslambano (G4355) — to take to oneself, receive; Romans 15:7.
usage: “receive ye one another” (Rom 15:7) — his case for open communion.
“in demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1Co 2:4) — the preacher's aim.
“they that gladly received his word were baptized” (Act 2:41) — the strict reply.

pos: n. (Joseph Charles Philpot, 1802–1869, Oxford fellow who seceded from the Church of England and edited the Strict Baptist Gospel Standard)
etymology: Hebrew Yoseph, he shall add; English Philpot, a diminutive of Philip.
biblical_def: Joseph Charles Philpot was a brilliant classical scholar, a fellow of Worcester College, Oxford, and curate of Stadhampton in Oxfordshire, where he came under deep conviction of sin and into an experimental knowledge of free grace. In 1835 he resigned his fellowship and left the Church of England, explaining his reasons in a public letter to the Provost of Worcester that went through many editions; he could not, he wrote, continue in a church whose services pronounced every baptized child regenerate and whose communion admitted the ungodly. He was baptized as a believer and for the rest of his life was a Strict Baptist minister, serving the churches at Stamford and Oakham. From 1849 until his death he edited the Gospel Standard magazine, and his sermons, reviews, and meditations made him the chief voice of the Strict Baptist churches of that name. He wrote with great beauty on the sufferings of Christ, the experience of the soul under law and gospel, and the eternal Sonship of Christ, which he defended in a notable treatise. He belonged also to the school that denied it is the duty of all men to believe the gospel. His conversion followed the psalmist's pattern: “Come and hear, all ye that fear God, and I will declare what he hath done for my soul” (Psa 66:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines secession as the act of withdrawing from fellowship, and experience as practical acquaintance with any matter.
webster_full: SECES'SION, n. The act of withdrawing, particularly from fellowship and communion.
EXPE'RIENCE, n. Practical acquaintance with any matter by personal observation or trial; trial of the heart in religious matters.
FEL'LOW, n. In a college, one of the corporation; a member who shares its revenues.
scriptures: Come and hear, all ye that fear God, and I will declare what he hath done for my soul.
Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
Joh 6:29
Jesus answered and said unto them, This is the work of God, that ye believe on him whom he hath sent.
And this is his commandment, That we should believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, as he gave us commandment.
corruption_summary: An Oxford fellow who left the established church for the Strict Baptists, and denied duty-faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the denial of duty-faith as an error, while honouring much in Philpot. Scripture commands sinners as such to believe: “this is his commandment, That we should believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ” (1Jn 3:23), and Christ told the unconverted crowd at Capernaum, “This is the work of God, that ye believe on him whom he hath sent” (Joh 6:29). A system that will not urge every hearer to come to Christ has let a deduction about inability override the command.

What is honourable in Philpot is equally clear. His secession was an act of conscience, made at great cost, against a church that pronounced every baptized infant regenerate, and his writing on Christ's sufferings and on the soul's experience under grace is among the richest of the century. The principle to recover is the one he held and the one he missed: experimental religion is necessary, and so is the free offer.
roots_summary: Greek pisteuo (G4100), to believe; entole (G1785), commandment; Hebrew saphar (H5608), to declare.
usage: “I will declare what he hath done for my soul” (Psa 66:16) — his experimental theology.
“come out from among them, and be ye separate” (2Co 6:17) — the letter to the Provost.
“this is his commandment, That we should believe” (1Jn 3:23) — the duty he denied.

pos: n. (John Warburton, 1776–1857, Lancashire weaver and Strict Baptist pastor at Trowbridge, author of The Mercies of a Covenant God)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; English Warburton, a Cheshire place-name.
biblical_def: John Warburton was a poor hand-loom weaver of Lancashire who was converted as a young man, joined a Particular Baptist church, and began to preach in cottages and chapels while still struggling to feed a large family. His autobiography, The Mercies of a Covenant God, published in 1837, records with unusual candour his poverty, his debts, his temptations and despairs, his deliverances, and the gradual opening of his way into the ministry. It became a devotional classic among English Strict Baptists, read for its account of the providences of God toward a man with nothing. In 1815 he became pastor of Zion Chapel at Trowbridge in Wiltshire, where he ministered for over forty years and where his preaching drew large congregations of working people. Warburton's theology was a high, experimental Calvinism: God's eternal covenant of grace, the soul's conviction under the law, deliverance by the gospel, and dependence on the Lord for every daily need. His life was a sermon on Moses' counsel to Israel: “thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee” (Deu 8:2). His book's refrain was the psalmist's: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psa 103:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a weaver as one who weaves, and mercy as that benevolence which overlooks injuries and treats an offender better than he deserves.
webster_full: WEA'VER, n. One who weaves, or whose occupation is to weave.
MER'CY, n. That benevolence, mildness or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries, or to treat an offender better than he deserves.
PROV'IDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
scriptures: Deu 8:2

And thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no.
Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:
Whoso is wise, and will observe these things, even they shall understand the lovingkindness of the LORD.
Come and hear, all ye that fear God, and I will declare what he hath done for my soul.
corruption_summary: A weaver-preacher whose autobiography told the providences of God to a poor man.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Warburton's book is a rebuke to two modern errors at once: the prosperity teaching that measures God's favour by comfort, and the secular reading of poverty that leaves God out of the account. He was poor for most of his life and testified that God was faithful in it, and the psalm describes the reader he hoped for: “Whoso is wise, and will observe these things, even they shall understand the lovingkindness of the LORD” (Psa 107:43).

The principle to recover is the value of the ordinary believer's testimony. The church has always been strengthened by the record of what God has done for plain men and women, and the command to tell it is old: “Come and hear, all ye that fear God” (Psa 66:16).
roots_summary: Hebrew zakar (H2142), to remember; anah (H6031), to humble; gemul (H1576), benefit.
usage: “remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee” (Deu 8:2) — the shape of his memoir.
“forget not all his benefits” (Psa 103:2) — the mercies of a covenant God.
“they shall understand the lovingkindness of the LORD” (Psa 107:43) — the reader's reward.

pos: n. (the controversy of 1887–1888 in which C. H. Spurgeon withdrew from the Baptist Union over its toleration of doctrinal error)
etymology: English down grade, a downward slope on a railway; Latin controversia.
biblical_def: The Downgrade Controversy takes its name from two articles titled The Down Grade published in Spurgeon's magazine The Sword and the Trowel in March and April 1887, written by his friend Robert Shindler. They traced the decline of English Presbyterians and General Baptists in the eighteenth century from orthodoxy into Arianism and Socinianism, and warned that the Nonconformist churches of the 1880s were sliding down the same incline. Spurgeon followed with articles of his own, charging that ministers in the Baptist Union were denying the inspiration of Scripture, the substitutionary atonement, and the reality of eternal punishment, and that the Union would not act. On 28 October 1887 he withdrew from the Baptist Union. In January 1888 the Union's council passed a vote of censure on him for making charges without naming names, and in April the assembly adopted a brief declaratory statement of evangelical doctrine, carefully worded to satisfy all parties, by an overwhelming majority, with Spurgeon's own brother James among its supporters. Spurgeon called it a creed without discipline, and never returned. He died in 1892, worn out, he believed, by the conflict. His charge was Paul's: “I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel” (Gal 1:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a controversy as a disputation, particularly a discussion of a question of doctrine.
webster_full: CON'TROVERSY, n. Debate; agitation of contrary opinions; a dispute in writing, especially on religious subjects.
CEN'SURE, n. The act of blaming or finding fault and condemning as wrong.
SOCIN'IANISM, n. The tenets or doctrines of Socinus, who denied the divinity of Christ and the atonement.
scriptures: Gal 1:6
I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel:
Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
Amo 3:3
Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
corruption_summary: Spurgeon's last battle: a union that would sign a creed but would not keep it.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the corruption Spurgeon fought as the toleration, within an evangelical union, of ministers who denied the inspiration of Scripture, the substitutionary atonement, and eternal punishment. The Union's answer, a vague statement and a censure of the man who raised the alarm, is the classic form of institutional drift. Paul foresaw it: “the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine” (2Ti 4:3).

The honest caveat is that Spurgeon's refusal to name names left him open to the charge of slander, and that some of his allies were harsher than he. But history vindicated him; the Union drifted precisely as he warned. The principle to recover is the one he died for: fellowship requires agreement in the gospel, “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3), and contending “for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jude 1:3) is a duty, not a temperament.
roots_summary: Greek metatithemi (G3346), to remove, transfer; heteros (G2087), another; anechomai (G430), to endure.
roots_lines: Greek heteros (G2087) — another of a different kind; Galatians 1:6.
Greek anechomai (G430) — to bear with, endure; 2 Timothy 4:3.
usage: “unto another gospel” (Gal 1:6) — the slope Spurgeon saw.
“they will not endure sound doctrine” (2Ti 4:3) — the Union's drift.
“earnestly contend for the faith” (Jude 1:3) — why he withdrew.

pos: n. (Susannah Spurgeon, née Thompson, 1832–1903, wife of C. H. Spurgeon and founder of the Book Fund for poor ministers)
etymology: Hebrew Shoshannah, a lily; English Spurgeon, of uncertain origin.
biblical_def: Susannah Thompson was a London merchant's daughter who first heard the young Charles Spurgeon preach at New Park Street Chapel in 1853, was converted under his ministry, and married him in January 1856. Their twin sons, Charles and Thomas, were born that September; both became Baptist ministers. From about 1868 she was an invalid, often confined to her room for long periods, and could seldom hear her husband preach. In 1875, after reading the first volume of his Lectures to My Students, she wished that every poor minister in England could have a copy, and her husband challenged her to see to it. The Book Fund she founded distributed, by her own hand and correspondence, some two hundred thousand volumes to pastors who could not afford books, in every denomination and many countries, and her accounts of it, Ten Years of My Life in the Service of the Book Fund, show a woman who turned her suffering into ministry to ministers. After her husband's death in 1892 she completed his four-volume Autobiography and founded a Baptist chapel at Bexhill. She is the woman of Proverbs, of whom “her husband also, and he praiseth her” (Pro 31:28), and the friend of Paul's need: “the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a wife as the lawful consort of a man, and an invalid as a person who is weak or infirm.
webster_full: WIFE, n. The lawful consort of man; a woman who is united to man in the lawful bonds of wedlock.
INVALID, n. A person who is weak and infirm; a person sickly or indisposed.
FUND, n. A stock or capital; a sum of money appropriated as the foundation of some commercial or other operation.
scriptures: Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments.
She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness.
corruption_summary: A minister's invalid wife who supplied two hundred thousand books to poor ministers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Susannah Spurgeon is sometimes recruited as an example of a woman finding her own ministry apart from her husband. Her own account is the opposite: she served her husband's calling and the calling of other pastors, from an invalid's room, and called it the joy of her life. Scripture's praise of the godly wife is her portrait: “a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised” (Pro 31:30).

The principle to recover is that suffering does not end usefulness. The Book Fund grew from a sickroom, and its letters show “in her tongue is the law of kindness” (Pro 31:26). A church that sees in chronic illness only loss has not considered how often God has worked through the bedridden.
roots_summary: Hebrew halal (H1984), to praise; yare (H3373), fearing; Greek biblion (G975), book.
usage: “her husband also, and he praiseth her” (Pro 31:28) — Spurgeon's tributes to his wife.
“the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13) — the Book Fund's text.
“in her tongue is the law of kindness” (Pro 31:26) — her letters to poor pastors.

pos: n. (Archibald Geikie Brown, 1844–1922, Spurgeon's student, pastor of the East London Tabernacle, and author of The Devil's Mission of Amusement)
etymology: Germanic Erkanbald, genuinely bold; English Brown, of brown complexion.
biblical_def: Archibald Brown was converted in his teens, trained at Spurgeon's Pastors' College, and in 1866 became pastor of a small Baptist church in Stepney that grew under his ministry into the East London Tabernacle, a congregation of some three thousand in one of the poorest districts of London. His work among the East End poor, through mission halls, relief for the destitute in the hard winters, and ministry to dock labourers and their families, was as remarkable as his preaching. He stood with Spurgeon throughout the Downgrade Controversy and was among his closest friends. He is best remembered for a pamphlet, The Devil's Mission of Amusement, in which he argued that providing entertainment to draw people to church was nowhere commanded by Christ, nowhere practised by the apostles, and wholly unable to do what the gospel does; the early church, he observed, turned the world upside down without it. From 1907 to 1911 Brown was pastor of the Metropolitan Tabernacle itself. His argument was the apostles': the Thessalonians “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1Th 1:9) under preaching, and the apostolic church “continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine” (Act 2:42).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines amusement as that which amuses, detains or engages the mind, entertainment.
webster_full: AMUSE'MENT, n. That which amuses, detains or engages the mind; entertainment of the mind; pastime.
TAB'ERNACLE, n. A tent; a place of worship; a sacred place.
DES'TITUTE, a. Not having or possessing; wanting; in need of the necessaries of life.
scriptures: For they themselves shew of us what manner of entering in we had unto you, and how ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God;
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
corruption_summary: An East End pastor who called church entertainment the devil's mission.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the corruption Brown attacked as the attempt to win the world to the church by entertainment, which has since become the method of much of evangelicalism. Brown's point was exegetical: Christ sent His disciples to preach, not to amuse, and His invitation is to rest in Him, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mat 11:28), not to diversion. A church that must entertain people to keep them has already conceded that the gospel is not enough.

His own ministry answers the objection that plain preaching cannot reach the poor. He preached the gospel in the poorest district in London to thousands, and fed the hungry beside it. The principle to recover is Paul's: power in preaching is “not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1Co 2:4).
roots_summary: Greek epistrepho (G1994), to turn; proskartereo (G4342), to continue stedfastly; anapauo (G373), to give rest.
roots_lines: Greek anapauo (G373) — to cause to rest, refresh; Matthew 11:28.
usage: “turned to God from idols” (1Th 1:9) — conversion without amusement.
“continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine” (Act 2:42) — what held the first church.
“I will give you rest” (Mat 11:28) — the gospel's offer, not the world's.

pos: n. (the Philadelphia Baptist Association, organized in 1707, the oldest Baptist association in America)
etymology: Greek philadelphia, brotherly love; Latin associatio, a joining as companions.
biblical_def: The Philadelphia Association was formed in 1707 by five Particular Baptist churches in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delaware: Pennepek, Middletown, Piscataway, Cohansey, and Welsh Tract. Their messengers met yearly for worship, counsel, and the settlement of questions brought by the churches, and the association grew to include congregations from New York to Virginia. It held that each church is complete in itself under Christ, but that churches of the same faith should hold communion, give one another advice in hard cases, and withdraw fellowship from a church that falls into heresy or disorder. In 1742 it adopted the Second London Confession, with two additional articles, as its doctrinal standard. It sent ministers and missionaries southward through the colonies, encouraged the training of ministers, and in 1764 was instrumental in founding the College of Rhode Island, later Brown University. The Philadelphia Association's confessional, associational Calvinism became the pattern for the Charleston Association and for much of the Baptist life of the early United States. Its pattern was the apostolic church, which “continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42), and the council at Jerusalem, whose letter began, “it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us” (Act 15:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an association as a society formed for transacting business, particularly an ecclesiastical body of churches.
webster_full: ASSOCIA'TION, n. Union of persons in a company or society, for some particular purpose; in ecclesiastical affairs, a society of the clergy, or of churches, consisting of a number of pastors or messengers.
MES'SENGER, n. One who bears a message; one sent by a church to an assembly.
COMMU'NION, n. Fellowship; union in religious worship, or in doctrine and discipline.
scriptures: Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things;
Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
Tit 3:10
A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;
corruption_summary: Colonial Particular Baptists joined in a confessional association for counsel and communion.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Philadelphia Association answers a modern Baptist assumption that congregational independence means isolation. The founders held both that each church is a complete church and that churches owe one another counsel and accountability, as at Jerusalem, where “the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6).

The principle to recover is confessional association. The association was bound together not by a programme or a budget but by a shared confession, and it could withdraw fellowship from churches that abandoned it, applying to churches the rule Paul gives for men: “A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject” (Tit 3:10).
roots_summary: Greek koinonia (G2842), fellowship; dokeo (G1380), to seem good; hairetikos (G141), heretic.
roots_lines: Greek dokeo (G1380) — to think, seem good; Acts 15:28.
usage: “the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42) — the ground of association.
“it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us” (Act 15:28) — counsel among churches.
“after the first and second admonition reject” (Tit 3:10) — withdrawal of fellowship.

pos: n. (the Baptist confession of faith adopted by the Philadelphia Association in 1742: the Second London Confession with two added articles)
etymology: Greek philadelphia, brotherly love; Latin confessio, an acknowledgment.
biblical_def: The Philadelphia Confession is the Second London Baptist Confession of 1677 and 1689, adopted by the Philadelphia Baptist Association in 1742 and printed in 1743 by Benjamin Franklin. The association had long used the London Confession informally; in 1742 it asked Jenkin Jones and Benjamin Griffith to prepare an American edition. They kept the text of the 1689 Confession and added two articles. The first, on singing of psalms in public worship, affirmed that singing the praises of God is an ordinance of Christ to be practised by the whole congregation, against those Baptists who opposed congregational singing. The second, on the laying on of hands, required that believers after baptism receive the laying on of hands with prayer, a practice the Welsh Baptists in the association held from Heb 6:2. The Confession became the standard of the Philadelphia and Charleston associations and of hundreds of Baptist churches in the colonies and the early republic, and through them the confessional Calvinism of the 1689 shaped American Baptist life until the nineteenth century. Its warrant for singing is Paul's: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Eph 5:19). Its article on hands rests on the apostle's list of first principles: “Of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands” (Heb 6:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession of faith as a formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised.
webster_full: CONFES'SION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a creed to be assented to or signed, as a preliminary to admission into a church.
AR'TICLE, n. A point of faith; a doctrinal point or proposition in theology.
IMPOSI'TION, n. The act of laying on; as the imposition of hands.
scriptures: Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
Heb 6:2
Of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands, and of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment.
Act 8:17
Then laid they their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost.
Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: The 1689 Confession in American dress, with articles on congregational singing and the laying on of hands.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Philadelphia Confession is a reminder that early American Baptists were confessional Calvinists, not the creedless individualists later histories imagined. They adopted an inherited confession whole and added to it only what their own controversies required, contending, as Jude urges, “for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jude 1:3).

The honest caveat concerns the second added article. The laying on of hands on every baptized believer as a standing ordinance was a distinctive of the Welsh churches; Act 8:17, where the apostles “laid they their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost” (Act 8:17), describes an apostolic sign rather than a perpetual rite, and most confessional Baptists have not retained it. The principle to recover is the one the whole Confession serves: a church's worship and order must be warranted by Scripture.
roots_lines: Greek psalmos (G5568) — a psalm, sacred song; Ephesians 5:19.
usage: “in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Eph 5:19) — the first added article.
“and of laying on of hands” (Heb 6:2) — the second.
“once delivered unto the saints” (Jude 1:3) — why they kept the London text.

pos: n. (the Charleston Baptist Association, organized in 1751, the first Baptist association in the American South)
etymology: Charleston, the South Carolina port named for Charles II; Latin associatio.
biblical_def: The Charleston Association was formed in 1751 by four Particular Baptist churches in South Carolina, led by the First Baptist Church of Charleston, whose roots went back to Baptists who had emigrated from Kittery in Maine in the 1690s. Its organizing spirit was Oliver Hart, who came from the Philadelphia Association in 1750 to be pastor at Charleston and modelled the new body on the one he knew. In 1767 it adopted the Second London Confession, in the form used at Philadelphia, as its confession of faith, and in 1774 it published a Summary of Church Discipline, a manual for the government of Baptist churches that set out the offices of pastor, elder, and deacon, the reception and dismissal of members, and the process of discipline from private admonition to excommunication. It sent missionaries into the backcountry, raised funds to educate ministers, and under Richard Furman in the next generation became the centre of organized Baptist life in the South. The Association's Summary made church discipline a matter of obedience to Christ, as Paul commanded the Corinthians, “put away from among yourselves that wicked person” (1Co 5:13), and its procedure followed Christ's own: “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines discipline in the church as the execution of the laws by which the church is governed.
webster_full: DIS'CIPLINE, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, the execution of the laws by which the church is governed, and infliction of the penalties enjoined against offenders.
EXCOMMUNICA'TION, n. The act of ejecting from a church; expulsion from the communion of a church.
ASSOCIA'TION, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, a society of the clergy, or of churches.

corruption_summary: The first Southern Baptist association, whose manual made church discipline ordinary.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption the Charleston Summary answers is the near-total disappearance of church discipline from modern Baptist life. Eighteenth-century Baptists disciplined members for drunkenness, sexual sin, fraud, and false doctrine as a matter of course, because Christ commanded it, and Paul's rule was not optional: “put away from among yourselves that wicked person” (1Co 5:13).

The honest caveat is that the same churches of the South later made peace with slavery and disciplined no man for holding slaves, which the dictionary names as a failure of the discipline they practised. The principle to recover is that discipline must be both faithful and impartial: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40).

pos: n. (Isaac Backus, 1724–1806, New England Baptist minister, historian, and champion of religious liberty)
etymology: Hebrew Yitschaq, he laughs; English Backus, a bakehouse.
biblical_def: Isaac Backus was converted in 1741 in Norwich, Connecticut, during the Great Awakening, and joined the Separate Congregationalists who left the established churches over unconverted ministers and lax membership. He became pastor of a Separate church at Middleborough, Massachusetts, but study of Scripture persuaded him that only believers should be baptized, and in 1756 he formed the First Baptist Church of Middleborough, which he served for fifty years. Massachusetts taxed every citizen for the support of the established Congregational ministry, and Baptists who would not pay were fined, imprisoned, or had their goods seized. Backus became their advocate. As agent of the Warren Association from 1772, he collected cases of persecution, petitioned the General Court, and wrote An Appeal to the Public for Religious Liberty (1773), arguing that civil and ecclesiastical government are distinct, that God has given the magistrate no authority over worship, and that taxing men to support a church is a usurpation of Christ's authority. In 1774 he pressed the Baptist case before the Massachusetts delegates to the Continental Congress. He also wrote a three-volume history of the New England Baptists. His distinction was Christ's: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines liberty of conscience as freedom from restraint in religious opinions and worship.
webster_full: LIB'ERTY, n. Religious liberty is the free right of adopting and enjoying opinions on religious subjects, and of worshiping the Supreme Being according to the dictates of conscience, without external control.
ESTAB'LISHMENT, n. The episcopal form of religion, so called, in England; any form of religion legally established and supported by the state.
AP'PEAL, n. A call upon a superior judge or court for a decision; a summons to answer to a charge.

corruption_summary: A Great Awakening convert who argued that Christ, not the colony, rules the church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Backus is now often enlisted for a secular separation of church and state that he would not have recognized. He did not want religion banished from public life; he wanted the magistrate to stop taxing Baptists for a church they could not in conscience support, and to leave worship to Christ. His argument was theological: the church is Christ's kingdom, and its support and government belong to Him and to His people, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).

The principle to recover is the distinction of the two governments, not the separation of God from either. Paul's word on liberty governs it: “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2Co 3:17), and that liberty is freedom to obey Christ without the state's coercion, not freedom from Christ.
